part: Legacy Contact on the Apple Accounts
problem: The card is about Jordan bringing Happy back after a power cut while Tony travels. A Legacy Contact only works after a death, with a death certificate, and Apple leaves saved passwords out of it, so it does nothing for this card's purpose.
checked: The card's own caveat 3 ('for the worst case, not for a business trip') and its Apple source on Legacy Contact (already listed on the card); roadmap section 9, Reboots row (By: You), which asks only for a way back after a power cut; no roadmap line or fact-sheet line mentions account inheritance.

proposal.text: Take the Legacy Contact sentence and its caveat out. The card is then: how to tell Happy is down, the envelope, unlock and log in, who to call, one rehearsal.

loses: A reminder to set up Apple's after-death account access, which is a personal estate matter and not a Happy feature.

part: 20 deny entries deployed in wave A for devices that are not paired
problem: No Mac or phone is paired, pairing already needs Tony's manual approval, and OpenClaw gives a newly paired device no commands until its command list is approved too. The list written now only guards against Tony's own later approvals, and the card says the real command names must be read from each device at pairing anyway.
checked: Installed docs/nodes/command-policy.md ('An initial unapproved surface has no effective commands', and the three requirements a command must meet); the card's own text that both pairing auto-approval keys are off in the config repo since M0; its unverified list (two side-effect checks on the live research browser and MCP servers, and an unknown phone command name); no roadmap rule covers paired devices; the only cards that pair anything are OCL-01 (wave D) and MAC-02 (later).

proposal.text: Deploy nothing in wave A. Make the deny list step 1 of whichever card first pairs a device (OCL-01 already says so), written from that device's declared command list. Keep one line in the config repo notes: no Mac app, no pairing and no setup link before that step.

loses: If Tony paired a Mac app before doing that step, its default commands (pointer control included) would be available after his two approvals. Nothing else while pairing stays manual.

part: extra happy-inspect lines (sshVerify, deny list, pluginTools, the cua-computer plugin)
problem: These lines check that Tony has not changed settings that only Tony can change, in a config that comes from a reviewed repo and is already compared with that repo after every deploy.
checked: Roadmap section 1b: the control plane is Tony's alone, plugin and config chat commands stay off, and happy-inspect already runs after every deploy next to the drift check; the card says both pairing keys are already in the config repo; no agent holds exec, so no agent can enable a plugin.

proposal.text: Keep the values in the config repo and let the existing drift check cover them. Add a posture line only when a device is actually paired.

loses: A named failure message if one of these values were edited in the repo itself.

part: full build design (virtual machine, desk agent, hook, file route, watching view, test gate) for a parked pilot
problem: The card says no family chore is approved for screen control, yet it specifies every piece of the build, and nine of those pieces are untested. The design will have to be redone around whatever chore is eventually named.
checked: The card's description ('no family task is approved for it today'), its last dependency ('none approved today') and its nine unverified points; frame.json decision 'Install the OpenClaw Mac app anywhere at all?' recommends no for this batch; the fact sheet has only Tony's example 'controlling a computer'; removed.json shows MAC-01, MAC-03, MAC-05 and MAC-15 were folded in during review; no roadmap milestone includes screen control.

proposal.text: Shrink the card to a parked note: what was learned (screen control needs the Mac app; never on Happy's own desktop; the vendors advise an isolated machine), the trigger to reopen it (a named chore that no app or script handles), and the first two things to test then (does control work inside a virtual machine; can the app run there without operator rights). Design the rest when the chore exists.

loses: The ready-made design text. It stays in the review history if it is wanted later.

part: desk hook: action allowlist, approval on the first action, kill-file check, target pin
problem: The card's own caveats say the action allowlist cannot stop a wrong click and the first-action approval only proves someone started the task; the virtual machine is the real limit. Where that approval prompt would arrive is unknown, and it may block every run.
checked: Card caveats 4 and 5; unverified points 1, 3 and 4; MAC-04 already lists three off switches and forbids the Gateway-desktop plugin, which is what the target pin guards; the card's example is an operator pilot that Tony starts and watches himself.

proposal.text: For an attended operator pilot use no hook: Tony starts each run, watches it, and stops it with the switch in the Mac app or by putting the deny line back. Add code checks only if a family member is ever allowed to start a run by text.

loses: 'Happy, stop everything' (G005) would not halt a desk run in mid-task; Tony would use the app switch.

part: ten-task acceptance test (8 of 10 on three runs, re-run after every update)
problem: A general ten-task exam with a pass bar is set before there is one real chore to test, and the card says a pass shows usefulness, not safety. The bar is called a suggestion and has no source.
checked: Card 'adds' text from MAC-05 ('the suggested bar') and caveat 8; fact sheet: evals run on demand and after a critical-path change, never on a schedule; removed.json lists MAC-05 as folded in under the category 'vague'.

proposal.text: When a chore is named, run that chore five times on the clean machine, once with a planted instruction on screen, and read the results. No general task set and no standing re-run.

loses: A broader picture of what screen control can do beyond the one chore.

part: the iPhone app as a second way to reach Happy

checked: Fact sheet (his example: 'a connected idle iPhone'); frame.json answer 'Can Happy control a connected idle iPhone?' ('No') and its decision on pairing the phone ('only if the share sheet, native approvals or Talk are worth it to you'); card caveat 3 and its 20 unverified points; no roadmap milestone names the iPhone app or Talk mode.

loses: The share sheet, the offline queue, the native approval inbox and Talk mode on Tony's phone.

part: step 4, realtime voice through an OpenAI voice model

checked: frame.json decision 'Voice: is any cloud speech acceptable?' recommends local only; removed.json: VOX-02 was folded in during round 2 with two of its dependencies pointing at entries that no longer exist; the roadmap's voice rows are local speech-to-text and text-to-speech; the fact sheet records no voice wish from Tony.

proposal.text: Delete step 4 with its dependency line, its caveat and its unverified point. If Talk is ever built and found too slow, raise realtime voice then as a new question.

part: branch for a second adult's phone (per-person identity with gateway.roles)
problem: The card says the app fits Tony's phone only, then carries a decision, a test-device step and three open checks for putting it on a second adult's phone.
checked: Card caveat 2 and safety text ('Tony's phone only'); frame.json decision on pairing recommends against both parents' phones; fact sheet: whether Jordan wants any of this was never stated.

loses: nothing

part: browser action firewall hook (profile, target and node pin, URL and nested-request parsing, 24-action allowlist)
problem: The research helper holds no family data, no memory and no logins, and the roadmap gives it a browser on exactly that ground. The hook is in-house code on the security boundary that needs a contract test after every OpenClaw update, and most of its checks repeat limits that config already sets.
checked: Roadmap section 5 table (research: no private data; its way out is the browser), the M3 exit gate (cannot change the recipient, cannot reach the LAN) and S5, where approval before form interaction and no submit apply to the jobs agent only; installed docs/tools/browser/agent-tools.md:39 (a sandboxed session cannot target the host browser unless allowHostControl is set), docs/gateway/sandboxing/docker-backend.md:91 (default false), docs/tools/browser/configuration.md SSRF section (navigation is pre-checked; private network off by default); removed.json: WEB-03 was written for a design with a site allowlist and typing approval, then folded in.

proposal.text: Use the roadmap's sandbox browser container with the LAN blocked, leave allowHostControl false and set evaluateEnabled false, all in config. If read-only in code is still wanted, the hook is one rule: block the `act` and `upload` actions for the research agent, failing closed. Drop the profile, target and node pin, the URL and nested-request parsing and the kind-mismatch check.

loses: A second, in-house copy of limits that config already sets. With no hook at all, an injected page could make the helper click or type on public sites while logged out; it has nothing private to type.

part: second reader: a host MCP wrapper around the summarize command-line tool
problem: The built-in page fetch already pulls the readable text out of articles, so the wrapper's only new gain is video captions and podcast transcripts, which nobody asked for. It runs on the host outside the built-in address checks, so the wrapper has to re-create them itself.
checked: Installed docs/tools/web-fetch.md:11 ('extracts readable content (HTML to markdown or text)'); card caveat 7 (runs on the host, outside the SSRF policy, with third-party fallbacks to switch off); the card's unverified points on summarize (the tool is not installed; its behaviour without captions is unknown); fact sheet: Tony's examples are web fetch and reading emails; roadmap M3 lists a browser and web fetch for research, not this tool.

proposal.text: Leave summarize out of this card. Build it only after a parent has actually asked for a video or podcast summary a few times; until then Happy says it cannot read videos.

loses: Main points from a captioned video, or from a podcast with a published transcript, given only a link.

checked: Fact sheet, 'Known from a scan, not from Tony' ('Tony has not said he wants any of them controlled'); card caveats 2 and 4 (devices come from the 9 Oct scan; neither tool is installed); no roadmap milestone covers house devices (the Home Assistant VM there is for the kids' speaker only).

checked: frame.json decision 'Home devices' recommends the command-line route; removed.json: HOM-01 was folded in during round 3; card caveat 5 ('pays off mainly if the announcements or the kids' kitchen speaker are also wanted'); roadmap section 9 'Kids voice' (By: You) plans the VM for the kids' speaker only, and the kids agent (F072) is parked; fact sheet: no Home Assistant install is known.

part: a separate stateless home agent reached by hand-off
problem: Every 'lights off' becomes two model turns and depends on a hand-off that has not yet been shown to return its result. The parent's own agent still decides when to hand off, so the extra agent does not stop a misled agent from switching things; the limits in the plugin code do.
checked:
Roadmap section 1 agent table (no home agent; reminders, notes and family logistics sit inside

-main) and section 5 (the trifecta is about private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out; a light switch and a favourites-only player send nothing out); F030 and F031 in r7.json put their in-house write tools directly on both parents' agents; roadmap section 1b lists hand-off results as not yet confirmed on this version.

proposal.text: Give the two plugin tools directly to each parent's own agent, as the Reminders bridge and the household store are, with the caps in the plugin. Have the tools return a fixed status ('on', 'off', 'playing') and no track titles.

loses: The parent's agent, which holds memory, gains two house tools; 'what is playing?' by title is left out so that agent reads no third-party text.

part: room allowlist, quiet hours and a night volume cap enforced in code
problem: Three code limits apply to a parent's own request, with numbers the card calls design numbers. As written, quiet hours on the Hue plugin could refuse 'downstairs lights off' at bedtime, which is the card's own example.
checked: Card unverified point 4 ('The volume caps (35, and 10 at night) are design numbers, not sourced'); fact sheet: quiet hours and preferred times were never stated by Tony; the 9 Oct scan shows two speakers, both in shared rooms; no roadmap rule covers house devices.

proposal.text: Keep one hard volume cap in the Sonos plugin, the one limit that bounds harm from a wrong or injected command. Drop quiet hours and the night cap for on-request commands, and add a room allowlist only when there is a room to exclude.

loses: A code block against lights or music being switched late at night by mistake.

proposal.text: Would a 'still on' text at night be useful, or is a lights-off time set in the Hue app enough? Default: drop the check and set the time in the Hue app.

Card safety text ('a way out', 'design requirements to build and test, not existing features') and unverified point 2; roadmap section 5 trifecta rule (

-main holds memory and reads search results, so it should gain no new way out); card description ('A phone on the home Wi-Fi can already print by itself').

part: one self-pacing scheduled job per project, with its own tools
problem: The check-in job picks its own gap, reads the note with tools and deletes itself, which needs an exception to the rule that timed jobs carry no tools, on top of a grant the vendor advises against. A fixed 'every three days' reminder gives the same nudge.
checked: Installed docs/automation/cron-jobs/schedules.md:19 and :67 (a plain fixed interval exists; pacing is optional); F007 in r7.json (recurring reminders with an empty tool list, already behind the recipient pin); card caveats 8 and 9 and its last dependency (the vendor guidance, and the open tool-list decision); the card's example asks only to 'check in with me every few days'; either design works for Jordan only if she becomes a command owner, which is F007's open question (fact sheet: 'No need' to add her to the command allowlist).

proposal.text: No new mechanism. A project is a note in the parent's memory (F041), one ordinary recurring reminder (F007) such as 'Party project: reply status for what is open', and one rule in the agent's instructions for keeping the note. The parent cancels the reminder when the project is done.

loses: The check-in text does not list the open items by itself (the parent replies to get them), Happy does not vary the gap, and the reminder is not removed automatically.
